nameStory: The name 'rue' comes from the Greek word 'reuo,' meaning 'to set free,' referring to its ancient reputation as a medicinal herb that could free people from ailments. It earned the nickname 'herb-of-grace' in medieval times because it was used in church ceremonies for sprinkling holy water, and people believed it could free the soul from sin.
description: Rue is a small, bushy perennial herb that grows about 2-3 feet tall with distinctive blue-green foliage. This Mediterranean native is grown in New England gardens primarily as an ornamental plant, prized for its unusual silvery-blue leaves that have a feathery, divided appearance. The plant produces small yellow flowers in summer and has a strong, somewhat bitter scent when the leaves are crushed. Despite being in the citrus family, rue looks nothing like an orange or lemon tree, instead resembling a compact, aromatic shrub.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Distinctive blue-green to silvery-blue leaves that are deeply divided into small, rounded segments, giving them a feathery or lacy appearance. The leaves feel somewhat thick and waxy to the touch and release a strong, bitter, almost medicinal smell when crushed.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small yellow flowers with four petals that bloom in flat-topped clusters during summer. Each tiny flower has a greenish center and the petals have a slightly cupped shape.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms a compact, rounded bush typically 2-3 feet tall and wide. The stems are somewhat woody at the base but remain herbaceous toward the tips, creating a neat, mounded appearance.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Produces small, rounded seed capsules that split open when ripe, revealing tiny black seeds. The capsules have a distinctive lobed appearance, almost like tiny crowns.

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Smooth, pale green stems that become somewhat woody with age. Young stems have the same blue-green tint as the leaves and contribute to the plant's overall silvery appearance.

habitat: In New England, rue is found almost exclusively in cultivated gardens, herb gardens, and around old homesteads where it has been planted as an ornamental or culinary herb. It thrives in well-drained, poor to average soils and can tolerate hot, dry conditions better than most garden plants. You're most likely to spot it in sunny locations where gardeners appreciate drought-tolerant plants with unusual foliage.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges with fresh blue-green foliage that's particularly striking. The distinctive divided leaves are the main identifying feature as the plant leafs out.
seasonality.summer: Peak identification time when small yellow flowers bloom in flat-topped clusters above the characteristic blue-green foliage. The strong scent of crushed leaves is most noticeable in warm weather.
seasonality.fall: Flowers fade and seed capsules develop, while the blue-green foliage may become slightly more silvery. In milder areas, the plant may remain semi-evergreen.
seasonality.winter: In protected locations, some foliage may persist, but the plant typically dies back to the ground. Look for woody stem bases that indicate where the plant will reemerge.

funFact: Despite being in the citrus family alongside oranges and lemons, rue contains compounds that can cause severe skin burns when combined with sunlight - a reaction called phototoxic dermatitis that can be worse than poison ivy and leave permanent scars, which is why experienced gardeners always wear gloves when handling it.
confusionNotes: Rue's blue-green, finely divided foliage might be confused with some ornamental artemisias (wormwoods), but rue's leaves are more rounded and segmented rather than thread-like, and rue has a much stronger, more bitter smell. Remember: rue has rounded leaf segments and yellow flowers, while artemisias have feathery leaves and tiny whitish flowers.
contextualKnowledge: Though called 'common rue,' this plant is actually quite uncommon in New England and should be handled with extreme caution due to its ability to cause severe skin burns in sunlight. Many gardeners are unaware of this danger and plant it simply for its attractive blue foliage, not realizing it requires careful handling and placement away from areas where people might brush against it.
compareHints: Rue is the only member of its genus found in New England gardens. Compared to other members of the citrus family, rue lacks the glossy, oval leaves typical of citrus plants and instead has its characteristic blue-green, deeply divided foliage. Unlike true citrus plants, rue is cold-hardy enough for New England gardens and produces small yellow flowers rather than the white, fragrant blooms of oranges and lemons.
